clinicalPearls: Odontogenic sinusitis is maxillary sinus inflammation arising from a dental source and accounts for a significant minority of maxillary sinus infections
It should be suspected in unilateral maxillary sinusitis, particularly when symptoms are refractory to standard rhinological treatment
A foul smell or taste and unilateral purulent discharge are characteristic clues pointing to a dental origin
Common causes include periapical infection of upper posterior teeth, periodontal disease, oroantral communication after extraction, and displaced roots or implants
The close relationship between the roots of maxillary premolars and molars and the sinus floor explains the spread of infection
Cone-beam CT is valuable for identifying the culprit tooth and the extent of sinus involvement
Effective treatment must address the dental cause, since sinus-directed therapy alone often fails
Management may combine dental treatment or extraction, closure of any oroantral communication, and sinus care in collaboration with ENT
reference.pathophysiology: Odontogenic sinusitis develops when the integrity of the barrier between the maxillary posterior teeth and the sinus floor is breached, allowing bacteria and inflammatory products to enter the sinus. This may follow periapical or periodontal infection extending through thin or dehiscent bone, an oroantral communication created during extraction, or displacement of roots, foreign material, or implants into the sinus. The resulting mixed, often anaerobic, infection disrupts mucociliary clearance and can obstruct the ostiomeatal complex, perpetuating sinus inflammation. Because the driver is dental, the process persists until the source is eliminated.
additionalInvestigations: Cone-beam or conventional CT to localise the dental source and sinus disease
Thorough dental examination with pulp testing of upper posterior teeth
Assessment for oroantral communication after recent extraction
Nasal endoscopy and ENT assessment where indicated
Culture of purulent discharge in resistant or severe cases
redFlags: Spread beyond the sinus with orbital swelling, visual changes, or signs of intracranial extension
Features suggesting invasive fungal sinusitis in immunocompromised or diabetic patients
Persistent unilateral disease or a mass raising suspicion of malignancy
Systemic sepsis from an odontogenic infection extending into deep spaces
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is good when the dental cause is identified and treated, with resolution of sinus symptoms; failure to address the source leads to persistent or recurrent sinusitis and occasional serious complications.
pitfalls: Treating recurrent unilateral maxillary sinusitis medically while missing the dental cause
Overlooking an oroantral communication after upper molar extraction
Failing to test the vitality of upper posterior teeth adjacent to the sinus
Neglecting displaced roots or implants within the sinus as a persistent nidus
management: Eliminate the dental source as the decisive step: extraction or endodontic (root-canal) treatment of the culprit tooth, or removal of displaced roots, implants or foreign material from the sinus
Surgical repair of any oroantral communication
Antibiotic therapy directed at the mixed aerobic-anaerobic flora, such as amoxicillin-clavulanate or a penicillin combined with metronidazole
Adjunctive nasal measures to restore drainage: saline irrigation, topical decongestants and intranasal corticosteroids
Endoscopic sinus surgery for persistent sinus disease or ostiomeatal obstruction after source control, with ENT input
Culture of purulent discharge to guide antibiotic choice in resistant or severe cases
Multidisciplinary dental/OMFS and ENT co-management, with vigilance for and escalation of orbital or intracranial spread

nodes.text: Unilateral maxillary sinusitis refractory to rhinological treatment; dental cause?
Red flag (orbital swelling, visual change, sepsis or intracranial spread)?
Escalate: urgent ENT and OMFS review for orbital or intracranial spread
CT or CBCT to localise the culprit tooth; pulp testing of upper posterior teeth
Is a dental source confirmed, such as periapical infection or oroantral communication?
Consider rhinogenic, allergic or fungal sinusitis, or a sinonasal tumour
Extraction or root-canal treatment of the culprit tooth; remove displaced roots
Surgical repair of any oroantral communication
Antibiotics for mixed flora: amoxicillin-clavulanate, or penicillin with metronidazole
Saline irrigation, decongestants and intranasal steroids to restore drainage
Endoscopic sinus surgery with ENT if disease persists after source control
